title: Acupressure Points: 11 Self-Care Points and How to Find Them — cv.cm
description: Where the 11 most used acupressure points are, with WHO 2008 locations and finger-widths, how hard and how long to press, and what the evidence really says.
h1: Acupressure points: where they are and how to press them
answer: Acupressure is a traditional practice of pressing set points on the body with the fingers. The most used self-care points are `LI4` on the hand, `PC6` on the inner wrist, `ST36` and `SP6` on the lower leg, `GB20` and `GB21` at the neck and shoulder, plus points on the feet and face. Press firmly but comfortably for 30 to 60 seconds. The best evidence is for `PC6` and nausea.

sections.h: What acupressure is, and what it is not
body: Acupressure comes from traditional Chinese medicine. It uses the same points as acupuncture, but you press them with a thumb or finger instead of a needle. Similar point pressing is part of shiatsu in Japan, of tuina massage in China, and of home remedies across Korea, Vietnam and Southeast Asia.

In the traditional view, the points sit along channels called meridians, and pressing them affects the flow of qi, a vital energy. These are traditional concepts. They are not structures that anatomy or physiology has found. A practical way to think about it: the points are useful, well-mapped places to press, often in a small hollow between muscles, tendons or bones.

The names can sound medical. `LI4` means point 4 on the Large Intestine channel, but pressing it has nothing proven to do with your bowel. The channel names are traditional labels. This page uses the point codes and locations from the WHO Standard Acupuncture Point Locations in the Western Pacific Region (2008), which lists 361 points. Taiyang, on the temple, is a traditional extra point outside that list; we use its usual description.

sections.h: How to find a point: cun and finger-widths
body: Point locations are measured in cun, a body-relative unit. Because it is relative, you measure with the fingers of the person being pressed, not with a ruler. For self-care, use your own fingers.

ul: 1 cun: the width of your thumb at the knuckle.
1.5 cun: your index and middle fingers held together.
2 cun: index, middle and ring fingers held together.
3 cun: all four fingers held together, measured across the middle knuckles.

body: The WHO standard measures most points by bone proportions, so finger-widths are an approximation. That is fine. A point is a small area, not a pinhead. When you are in the right place, you usually feel one of these: a slight hollow, a groove between two tendons or bones, or a spot that feels a little tender or gives a dull, spreading ache when pressed. If the spot feels the same as everything around it, move a few millimetres and try again.
These points appear in most acupressure guides because they are easy to reach on yourself. Press both sides of the body unless the table says otherwise.

sections.h: How to press: pressure, angle and time

ol: Sit or lie comfortably. Keep your nails short and your hands warm.
Find the point using the landmarks above.
Place the pad of your thumb or middle finger on it, not the tip or the nail.
Press straight in, at a right angle to the skin, unless the table gives an angle.
Build up the pressure slowly over about 5 seconds.
Hold steady, or make small circles about one per second, for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe slowly.
Release slowly over a few seconds.
Repeat 2 to 3 times, then do the other side.

body: Use a 1 to 10 pressure scale, where 1 is barely touching and 10 is the most pressure you could bear. Aim for 4 to 6: firm but not painful. In words:

ul: Light: the skin moves, the muscle underneath does not. Use this on the face, the inner wrist and fragile skin.
Medium: you feel the muscle move under your finger.
Firm: deeper, still comfortable, and you can breathe normally. Use this only on thick muscle, such as the lower leg or the sole.

body.note: A dull ache that feels good is fine. Sharp, burning or electric pain, numbness or tingling means you are pressing too hard or on a nerve. Stop, move slightly and use less pressure.

body: To time each hold without counting, you can use a timer, for example cv.cm's countdown set to 60 seconds.
This routine uses points that are easy to reach while sitting. Do it once a day, or when you take a break from a desk.

body: The strongest evidence is for `PC6` and nausea after surgery. A 2025 Cochrane review pooled 77 trials with 9,847 participants. Non-needle methods such as acupressure wristbands may reduce nausea and vomiting after surgery compared with a sham, and they may reduce the need for extra anti-sickness drugs. The reviewers rated the confidence as low, and they found only minor side effects such as skin irritation. These trials were in hospitals, with trained staff, and often alongside medicines. They do not show that `PC6` works for every kind of nausea.

For pain, a 2014 systematic review found 15 studies of acupressure for problems such as period pain, low back pain and chronic headache, with mostly positive results. The studies were small and varied in quality, so the review is a starting point, not proof.

NCCIH, the US government research centre for complementary health, reports moderate-quality evidence that acupuncture with needles may reduce how often migraines happen, and moderate- to low-quality evidence that it may reduce how often tension headaches happen. Acupressure has been studied much less than needles, and results from needles do not automatically apply to finger pressure. Part of any benefit is likely to come from relaxation, attention and expectation. Use acupressure as a calm, low-cost self-care habit, not as a replacement for medical care.

sections.h: Safety: when not to press, and when to see a doctor

ul: Do not press on broken, infected or burned skin, a rash, a fresh bruise or a recent injury.
Varicose veins: no deep pressure on the lower leg, including `SP6` and `ST36`.
Blood thinners or a bleeding disorder: light pressure only, because you may bruise.
Osteoporosis: no hard pressure on bone, such as the shin.
Diabetes with numb feet: check the skin of the feet before and after, and use light pressure on `KI1` and `LR3`.
Recent surgery, a fever, or cancer treatment: ask your care team first. Gentle touch is often fine.
Never press the front of the neck, the eyeballs, the spine itself or the back of the knee.

body.note: Pregnancy: traditional acupressure advice avoids firm pressure on `LI4`, `SP6` and `GB21` during pregnancy. If you are pregnant, ask your midwife or doctor before using acupressure. This page does not give pregnancy instructions.

body: See a doctor if the problem you are pressing for keeps coming back or gets worse. For nausea, get medical help if you cannot keep fluids down, the vomit contains blood, or you have severe stomach pain. Chest pain, sudden weakness on one side or a sudden severe headache are emergencies: call your local emergency number instead of trying points.

sections.h: Common mistakes and how to fix them

ul: Pressing too hard: if the area is sore the next day, halve the pressure and the time.
Using the fingertip or nail: switch to the flat pad of the thumb or finger.
Hunting for one exact spot: the point is a small area. Find the slight hollow and stay there.
Holding your breath: breathe slowly through the hold. Tension in the jaw and shoulders works against you.
Expecting a fixed result: notice how you feel after a week of short daily sessions, and stop if it does not help.

faq.a: For nausea after surgery, studies of `PC6` wristbands suggest a modest benefit, with low-confidence evidence. For pain and stress the studies are small and mixed. Many people find pressing points relaxing, which can be worthwhile on its own.

faq.q: Which pressure point is used for stress and anxiety?
faq.a: Traditional guides most often use Shenmen (`HT7`) on the wrist crease and Yintang (`GV29`) between the eyebrows, pressed lightly with slow breathing. The evidence is limited. Acupressure is not a treatment for an anxiety disorder; talk to a doctor if anxiety affects daily life.

faq.q: Can acupressure wristbands help with travel sickness?
faq.a: The wristbands press on `PC6`. The best studies are of nausea after surgery, and results for motion sickness are mixed. They are low-risk to try, but they should not replace medicine your doctor or pharmacist recommends.

faq.q: How often can I do acupressure?
faq.a: Short sessions of 3 to 10 minutes once or twice a day are typical. Give the skin and muscle a rest if a spot feels bruised or sore.

faq.q: Why does a pressure point hurt when I press it?
faq.a: Many points sit in hollows near tendons, nerves or tight muscle, so a dull tenderness is common. Sharp, burning or tingling pain means too much pressure or a nerve; ease off or move slightly.

faq.q: Is acupressure the same as reflexology?
faq.a: No. Acupressure uses points along the traditional meridians all over the body. Reflexology uses a map of zones on the feet and hands that is said to mirror the body. Both are traditional systems, not anatomy.
